name: Builder
intent: Construct a complex object step by step, so the same process can build different results and the call reads clearly.
scenario: A pizza shop builds pizzas with a size, crust, optional extra sauce and any toppings. A menu offers ready-made recipes like Margherita.
problem: Pizza has many parts, most optional. A constructor with six positional arguments is unreadable (true, false, true...) and every new option adds another parameter or another constructor overload.
solution: Move construction into a Builder with one named method per part and a build() at the end. Callers set only what they need, in readable steps. build() validates and returns the finished object. A Director can store common recipes.
pain: new Pizza("large", "thin", true, ["ham"], false) is hard to read
Callers must pass every argument, even defaults
Adding an option changes every call site
Nothing validates the combination before the object exists
benefits: Named steps make each call self-explanatory
Defaults live in the builder; callers set only what differs
A new option is one new builder method
build() is a single place to validate
whenToUse: Objects with many optional parameters or configuration steps
The same construction process must produce different representations
You want immutable results assembled in stages: HTTP requests, queries, documents
whenNotToUse: Objects with two or three simple fields: a constructor is clearer
Your language already has named and optional parameters that solve the problem
The extra builder class would be the largest part of the code
pitfalls: Forgetting to call build() and passing the half-built builder around
Reusing one builder for two objects without resetting it
Required fields that are only checked at runtime, not by the compiler
Boilerplate: the builder mirrors the product's fields

roles.label: Director
roles.description: Knows common recipes and drives a builder through them.

roles.label: Builder
roles.description: Offers a step per part and a build() method.
